newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries lower at midday, losing early gains.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries lower at midday, losing early gains.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were lower at midday on Wednesday, having wiped out small early gains as the dollar retreated and corporate supply weighed on prices, participants said.
The 30-year Treasury bond, which was up 4/32 and yielding 6.76 percent in early dealings in a firmness analysts tied to dollar strength, was down 9/32 to 96-8/32, yielding 6.79 percent near midday.
"We're still rangebound," observed Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Traders said the need to hedge corporate supply weighed on Treasury prices.
The size of US West Inc unit US West Capital Funding's multi-tranche debt offering was bumped to $3.5 billion on Wednesday from its initially planned size of $2.0 billion.

"There's a couple of deals coming to market that need to be hedged up," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc. "That's weighing on the market. We seem to be sufferig under the weight of supply."
The bond market also lost some support as the dollar moved lower, participants said.
The dollar retreated below 1.59 marks after touching 1.60 marks, its highest level since July 1994, and holding above 117 yen, near a fresh 46-month high, in early U.S. trade.
News that November business inventories rose 0.1 percent, below economists' average forecast of 0.3 percent, came out in as the market had started to erase its early gains.
But traders had called the data "secondary" and unlikely to move the market and they accorded the report minimal significance when it came out.
"Whether or not business inventories are up 0.1 percent or up 0.2 percent is absolutely irrelevant," contended Joseph Benning, trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

"Today is like Monday when the market was waiting for data to come out," said Alexy. "No one wants to get involved in a big way. They're waiting for more road signs -- (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan's testimony next week, the ECI (Employment Cost Index) the week after that and the (January) Purchasing Managers (report) the week after that."
Meanwhile, players just want to sell securities and buy them back at the extremes of the trading range, Alexy said.

Noting that Wednesday's decline followed a Tuesday's rally on a subdued core December Consumer Price Index (CPI), Benning said, "Some of the boys must have realized they got into 'irrationally exuberant' territory again.
"The market's real thin," he added. "It doesn't take much to move it one way or the other."

Another consideration that will start to creep into the market this afternoon is supply. The Treasury is scheduled to announce terms of its next set of monthly two- and five-year note auctions this afternoon.
At midday, two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-18/32, yielding 5.99 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.02 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.08 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.29 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-18/32, yielding 5.99 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 to 99-6/32, yielding 6.32 percent. Ten-year notes were down 6/32 to 99-22/32, yielding 6.54 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
